subject: chemistry
title: Ion
summary: An ion is an atom that has gained or lost electrons, giving it an electric charge. Sodium becomes Na⁺ by losing an electron; chlorine becomes Cl⁻ by gaining one.

compareCandidate.label: Ion vs. isotope
compareCandidate.description: An ion is an atom with a different electron count — same element, different charge. An isotope is an atom with a different neutron count — same element, different mass. Electrons change the charge; neutrons change the weight.

parts: Made by gaining or losing electrons
plainLanguageExplanation: An ion is an atom that carries an electric charge because it has gained or lost electrons. Normally an atom has equal protons and electrons — equal positive and negative — so it is neutral. But electrons can leave or arrive. If an atom LOSES an electron, it has more protons than electrons, so it becomes positive: a cation, like sodium becoming Na⁺. If an atom GAINS an electron, it has more electrons than protons, so it becomes negative: an anion, like chlorine becoming Cl⁻. Why does this happen? Atoms push toward full outer shells. Sodium, with one lonely outer electron, is eager to drop it and become a stable Na⁺. Chlorine, one electron short, eagerly grabs one and becomes Cl⁻. And here is the payoff: opposite charges attract. The positive Na⁺ and negative Cl⁻ snap together — that is the ionic bond that builds table salt. Ions are everywhere: dissolved in your blood, in batteries, in seawater, and driving the signals in your nerves. An ion is just an atom with a charge — a particle that has gained or lost a little electric edge.

whyItMatters: Ions are charged atoms, and charges drive much of the world: the salt on your table, the signals in your nerves, the batteries in your phone, and the reactions in your body. Understanding ions connects atomic structure to real chemistry — and sets up ionic bonding.
didYouKnow: Your nerves send messages using ions — a lightning-fast dance of sodium and potassium ions rushing in and out of your nerve cells.
compareReason: Ions change electrons and isotopes change neutrons — comparing these two variations of the same atom makes the difference between charge and mass unforgettable.
